bibl.title: Short-term implicit memory: Visual, auditory, and cross-modality priming

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: These modality differences suggest that short-tenn priming has a perceptual locus, with the phonological lexicon maintaining stimuli active longer than the ortho graphic lexicon and treating pseudowords as potential words.

span.label: short-term repetition priming
span.quote: Short-tenn implicit memory was examined for mixed auditory (A) and visual (V) stimuli.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: In lexical decision, words and nonwords were repeated at lags of 0, 1, 3, and 6 intervening trials, in four prime target combinations (yV, VA, AV, AA).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: because continuous speech is ambiguous and many apparent nonwords later resolve into words, the phonological lexicon must keep pseudoword-status items active as long as word-status items, producing slow auditory decay for both
span.quote: The phonologicallexi con, therefore, has need to hold items assigned pseudo word status active for as long as those assigned word sta tus: In continuous speech, many "nonwords" will later turn out to be real words.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: because the written signal is far less ambiguous, the orthographic lexicon can discard a nonword as soon as the next item arrives, producing the fast visual nonword decay
span.quote: The orthographic lexicon can afford, therefore, to rapidly discard a non word when the next item is presented.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: each stimulus is obligatorily recoded into the other perceptual form, and the secondary trace left by that recoding supports the weak cross-modal short-term priming
span.quote: The results sug gest that each stimulus undergoes obligatory recoding into the alternative perceptual form (i.e., orthographic to phonological and, more interestingly, vice versa), and that a secondary trace of this recoding can contribute to short-term priming.

span.label: Because no lags beyond 6 were tested, the authors cannot show that the long-term asymptote had actually been reached for auditory items.
span.quote: Priming at lag 6 reached the 20-50 msec range, at which we might expect long-term priming to stabilize for low-frequency words, but the in clusion of no longer lags means that there is no direct ev idence that the long-term value was attained by lag 6.

span.label: The orthographic locus previously assumed for visual short-term priming was never established directly, since words and pseudowords also differ phonologically and semantically.
span.quote: However, we have no direct evidence that the locus for written stimuli is specifically orthographic: Words and pseudowords also differ in their phonological and semantic familiarity status.

span.label: The locus assumed in the authors' own earlier explanations is stated to have no direct evidence, and a confound is named in the same sentence.
span.note: what this limits: the orthographic locus assumed in the authors' earlier accounts of short-term priming: they state there is no direct evidence for it and that words and pseudowords also differ phonologically and in semantic familiarity
span.quote: However, we have no direct evidence that the locus for written stimuli is specifically orthographic: Words and pseudowords also differ in their phonological and semantic familiarity status.

span.label: The obvious definition of the measured quantity is rejected outright, because unprimed response times differ by modality, and a different baseline is substituted.
span.note: what this limits: any comparison of these priming magnitudes with a study that measures priming as first-versus-second presentation: this paper rejects that definition and uses the mean of all unprimed trials of matching lexicality and modality as the baseline
span.quote: Thus, priming cannot be taken as the difference in RTs between the first and second presentations of the same item, particularly in the cross-modal conditions. Instead, we followed the procedure of Kirsner and Smith (1974) in choosing the baseline for priming to be the mean of all unprimed trials of the appropriate lexicality and modal ity.

span.label: lexical decision times below 300 or above 1,700 msec excluded, along with incorrect responses - 1.3 per cent of reaction times
span.note: eliminates: anticipations and lapses of attention dominating a mean, with the exclusion rate reported so a reader can see how much was removed
span.quote: Lexical decision times were excluded if they fell below 300 or above 1,700 msec (1.3% ofRTs), or ifan incorrect response was given to either presentation of the item (6.2% ofRTs).

span.label: implicit memory
span.quote: where implicit memory refers to auto matic retrieval of the target's initial presentation and is contrasted with the deliberate conscious retrieval re quired for explicit memory

span.label: explicit memory
span.quote: the deliberate conscious retrieval re quired for explicit memory revealed in recall and old new recognition tasks

span.label: short-term implicit memory
span.quote: We refer to this effect as short-term implicit memory, where the label short-term was chosen to reflect its similarity in duration to that of standard ex plicit short-term or "working" memory

span.label: baseline for priming
span.quote: Instead, we followed the procedure of Kirsner and Smith (1974) in choosing the baseline for priming to be the mean of all unprimed trials of the appropriate lexicality and modal ity.

span.label: short-term implicit memory - a name chosen by ANALOGY OF DURATION with explicit short-term memory, not by a claim about mechanism
span.quote: We refer to this effect as short-term implicit memory, where the label short-term was chosen to reflect its similarity in duration to that of standard ex plicit short-term or "working" memory

span.label: short-term implicit memory - and the commitment the name would carry is DECLINED in the next sentence: separate stores are explicitly not assumed
span.quote: We do not assume that different stores sub serve short- and long-term priming. Our preferred theo retical interpretation is of two mechanisms operating within a common system

span.label: priming - operationalised as the difference from the mean of ALL unprimed trials of matching lexicality and modality, after the first-versus-second-presentation definition was rejected
span.quote: Instead, we followed the procedure of Kirsner and Smith (1974) in choosing the baseline for priming to be the mean of all unprimed trials of the appropriate lexicality and modal ity.

span.label: implicit memory - automatic retrieval of the target's initial presentation, defined by CONTRAST with the deliberate conscious retrieval required for explicit memory
span.quote: where implicit memory refers to auto matic retrieval of the target's initial presentation and is contrasted with the deliberate conscious retrieval re quired for explicit memory

span.label: replicates → McKone (1995)
span.quote: First, the results of McKone (1995) were replicated when both presentations were visual, although the list used here contained mixed auditory and visual stimuli.

span.label: extends → Kirsner and Smith (1974)
span.quote: Our experiment was similar to that ofKirsner and Smith, but specifically targeted the region in which the lag X lexicality interaction is found with visual presentation.

span.label: contradicts → Kirsner and Smith (1974)
span.quote: Few studies have used auditory targets, but we note that our small ef fect appears to conflict with Kirsner and Smith's (1974) large cross-modal reduction in long-term priming in lex ical decision (83 vs. - 14 msec, for words at lags 15 and 63).

span.label: implicit memory —contrasted-with→ explicit memory
span.quote: where implicit memory refers to auto matic retrieval of the target's initial presentation and is contrasted with the deliberate conscious retrieval re quired for explicit memory

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: A repeated mea sures two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) confirmed a significant lag X lexicality interaction [F(3,63) = 2.76, MSe = 2,416, P < .05].

span.label: mean squared error
span.quote: A repeated mea sures two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) confirmed a significant lag X lexicality interaction [F(3,63) = 2.76, MSe = 2,416, P < .05].

span.label: planned contrasts (Helmert)
span.quote: Helmert contrasts were used to confirm the existence of some short-term priming in the cross-modal condi tions and to track the form of its decay.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Collapsing over lexicality, the cross-modal reduction in priming was significant for visual targets [31 vs. 2 msec, t(21) = 3.57, p < .005], but not for auditory targets (36 vs. 27 msec, t < 1).

span.label: three-way ANOVA
span.quote: A three-way ANOVA on the lag 6 data confirmed an interaction between modality of first presentation and modality of second presentation [F(l,2I) = 5.08, MSe = 3,033,p < .04], with no interac tions involving lexical status (all Fs < I).

span.label: four-way ANOVA with alpha level
span.quote: A four-way ANOVA revealed no significant in teractions (alpha = .05).

span.label: mean
span.quote: Instead, we followed the procedure of Kirsner and Smith (1974) in choosing the baseline for priming to be the mean of all unprimed trials of the appropriate lexicality and modal ity.

span.label: With visual stimuli, short-term priming decayed faster for nonwords than for words (a lag by lexicality interaction), whereas with auditory stimuli both item types decayed smoothly and slowly.
span.quote: Same-modality repetition priming showed a lag x lexicality inter action for visual stimuli (nonwords decayed faster), but not for auditory stimuli (longer lasting smooth decay for both words and nonwords).

span.label: Short-term priming lasted longer when both presentations were spoken than when both were written.
span.quote: Second, short-term auditory priming was shown to be longer lasting than short-term visual priming.

span.label: Auditory nonword priming survived at least three intervening trials (about 8 seconds), while visual nonword priming fell to its long-term level after a single intervening item.
span.quote: Third, the increased duration for auditory items was particularly striking for nonwords: whereas vi sual presentation produced decay to the long-term value with a single intervening item, auditory presentation pro duced a short-term priming effect for nonwords that en dured at least three intervening trials (8 sec) and decayed in exactly the same manner as for words.

span.label: Switching modality between prime and target reduced short-term priming but never abolished it, for words and nonwords alike.
span.quote: Fourth, short term priming was reduced by modality shift, but did not disappear completely; this general pattern was observed for both words and nonwords.

span.label: Cross-modal short-term priming persisted to lag 1 for word targets but disappeared after one intervening item for nonwords.
span.quote: Short-term cross modal priming endured to lag I when the target was a word, but cross-modal priming for nonwords dropped to the long-term value with a single intervening item.

span.label: The surviving cross-modal priming implies that a stimulus is recoded into the other perceptual form rather than that priming is stored centrally.
span.quote: Weak cross-modality short-tenn priming was present for words and nonwords, indicating recoding between perceptual fonns.

span.label: At lag 6, modality mismatch cut long-term priming from 31 to 2 msec for visual targets but left auditory targets essentially unaffected.
span.quote: Collapsing over lexicality, the cross-modal reduction in priming was significant for visual targets [31 vs. 2 msec, t(21) = 3.57, p < .005], but not for auditory targets (36 vs. 27 msec, t < 1).

span.label: Accuracy improved rather than worsened on repeated presentations, so the reaction-time priming was not a speed-accuracy trade-off.
span.quote: Error rates dropped from 11.3% on first presentation to 6.0% on second presentation for words, and from 5.9% to 5.7% fornonwords.

span.label: Unprimed lexical decisions were roughly 320-350 msec faster for written than for spoken items, so priming could not be computed as a raw first-versus-second difference.
span.quote: Unprimed responses were much faster to visual stim uli than to auditory stimuli (words: V = 620 msec, A = 966 msec; nonwords: V = 688 msec, A = 1,007 msec).

span.label: Responses to an item were faster when the immediately preceding trial was in the same modality, which biases the lag 0 baseline if it is ignored.
span.quote: A post hoc split of our data showed that first presentation RTs were consistently faster to trials that matched the preceding trial in modality.

span.label: The main locus of short-term priming is the perceptual subsystem in which the item was presented: orthographic for written items, phonological for spoken ones.
span.quote: Our results from the same-modality conditions indi cate that the primary locus for short-term priming is the perceptual subsystem to which the stimulus is presented (i.e., orthographic lexicon for V, phonological lexicon for A).

span.label: short-term implicit memory
span.quote: We refer to this effect as short-term implicit memory, where the label short-term was chosen to reflect its similarity in duration to that of standard ex plicit short-term or "working" memory (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974).

span.label: long-term implicit memory
span.quote: We refer to this type of priming as long-term im plicit memory, where implicit memory refers to auto matic retrieval of the target's initial presentation and is contrasted with the deliberate conscious retrieval re quired for explicit memory revealed in recall and old new recognition tasks (Graf & Schacter, 1985).

span.label: orthographic lexicon and phonological lexicon
span.quote: Two of these are percep tual in nature, namely the orthographic lexicon (for writ ten words; Schacter, 1994, calls this the visual word form system) and the phonological lexicon (for spoken words).

span.label: pseudoword (nonword)
span.quote: Stimuli were four-letter, single-syllable words and pseudowords (nonwords satisfying the rules of English, e.g., sime).

span.label: lag (0, 1, 3 or 6 intervening items)
span.quote: Lexical status (word, nonword) was crossed with first presentation modality (auditory, visual), second presentation modality (auditory, visual), and lag (0, 1,3, or 6 items intervening between repeats).

span.label: lexical status (word vs. nonword)
span.quote: Lexical status (word, nonword) was crossed with first presentation modality (auditory, visual), second presentation modality (auditory, visual), and lag (0, 1,3, or 6 items intervening between repeats).

span.label: modality of the first (prime) presentation
span.quote: Lexical status (word, nonword) was crossed with first presentation modality (auditory, visual), second presentation modality (auditory, visual), and lag (0, 1,3, or 6 items intervening between repeats).

span.label: modality of the second (target) presentation
span.quote: Lexical status (word, nonword) was crossed with first presentation modality (auditory, visual), second presentation modality (auditory, visual), and lag (0, 1,3, or 6 items intervening between repeats).

span.label: lexical decision reaction time
span.quote: Reaction time (RT) was recorded from the onset of the stimulus.

span.label: repetition priming magnitude (baseline RT minus repeated RT)
span.term: repetition priming magnitude (baseline RT minus repeated RT)
span.quote: For example, priming in the lag I AV word condition was calculated as the mean RT to second presentations in this condition, subtracted from the mean RT to first pre sentations ofall visually presented words (i.e., 620 msec).

span.label: error rate
span.quote: Error rates dropped from 11.3% on first presentation to 6.0% on second presentation for words, and from 5.9% to 5.7% fornonwords.

span.label: word frequency (all targets low frequency)
span.quote: The 320 tar get words were low frequency (1-15 per million; Kucera & Francis, 1967) and excluded proper nouns, extremely unfamiliar words, and words with ambiguous translation from orthography to phonology (e.g., wind) or vice versa (e.g., reed/read), so it was clear which word was being primed in the cross-modality conditions.

span.label: item length and syllable structure (four letters, one syllable)
span.term: item length and syllable structure (four letters, one syllable)
span.quote: Stimuli were four-letter, single-syllable words and pseudowords (nonwords satisfying the rules of English, e.g., sime).

span.label: modality of the immediately preceding trial in the lag 0 baseline
span.term: modality of the immediately preceding trial in the lag 0 baseline
span.quote: Instead, the baselines used for lag 0 priming were the values given in the previous paragraph: For example, second presentation RTs in the lag 0 AV word condition were compared with the mean RT to first presentations of vi suaI words preceded by auditory trials (i.e., 646 not 620 msec).

span.label: order of priming conditions and assignment of items to conditions
span.term: order of priming conditions and assignment of items to conditions
span.quote: The order of priming conditions was rerandom ized for every block for every subject.

span.label: V = 620 msec, A = 966 msec — unprimed lexical decision times for visual versus auditory words
span.quote: Unprimed responses were much faster to visual stim uli than to auditory stimuli (words: V = 620 msec, A = 966 msec; nonwords: V = 688 msec, A = 1,007 msec).

span.label: F(3,63) = 2.76, MSe = 2,416, P < .05 — the lag by lexicality interaction for same-modality visual priming
span.quote: A repeated mea sures two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) confirmed a significant lag X lexicality interaction [F(3,63) = 2.76, MSe = 2,416, P < .05].

span.label: 31 vs. 2 msec, t(21) = 3.57, p < .005 — same-modality versus cross-modality long-term priming at lag 6 for visual targets
span.quote: Collapsing over lexicality, the cross-modal reduction in priming was significant for visual targets [31 vs. 2 msec, t(21) = 3.57, p < .005], but not for auditory targets (36 vs. 27 msec, t < 1).

span.label: 11.3% to 6.0% — word error rates on first versus second presentation
span.quote: Error rates dropped from 11.3% on first presentation to 6.0% on second presentation for words, and from 5.9% to 5.7% fornonwords.

span.label: 22 — number of subjects tested
span.quote: Subjects were 22 volunteers with English as their first language.

span.label: 1,500 trials in five blocks of 300 — length of the trial list each subject completed
span.quote: The list for each subject comprised 1,500 trials in five blocks of 300.

span.label: 32 priming conditions ... with 20 items in each — design size: crossings of lexicality, prime modality, target modality and lag, with items per cell
span.quote: There were 32 priming conditions (see Design section) with 20 items in each.

span.label: 1.3% ofRTs / 6.2% ofRTs — proportion of responses discarded as outliers and as errors respectively
span.quote: Lexical decision times were excluded if they fell below 300 or above 1,700 msec (1.3% ofRTs), or ifan incorrect response was given to either presentation of the item (6.2% ofRTs).
